fixes.explanation: True. James says the elders should "…pray over him and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord." The sick person is the one who calls them. The prayer and the oil are both right there, and the verse ends with "in the name of the Lord."

Shepherds do show up in the Bible (Luke 2:8), but James doesn't point to one here. He points to a farmer who awaits the precious fruit of the soil. The shepherd can sit this one out and keep an eye on his flock. This picture is all about crops and waiting.
Judge. James says, "Look, the Judge is standing at the door!" He says it right after telling the brothers not to complain about one another. It's a serious line, and Judge is the word James picks.
A King is a fine title, and the Bible does call God King elsewhere (Psalm 47:7). But in this verse James says, "Look, the Judge is standing at the door!" The word he uses here is Judge.

Priests did serve in the temple (Luke 1:8–9), but James doesn't point to them here. He says, "…take the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord." The prophets are his example of patience in affliction.

Kings are a big part of Israel's story (1 Samuel 11:15), but James doesn't bring them up here. He holds up "…the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord." as his example of patience in affliction. Nobody gets a crown in this verse.

Job is the man. James says, "You have heard of Job’s perseverance and have seen the outcome from the Lord." He puts the perseverance and the outcome side by side. I think that's the kind of story you tell someone who's tired of waiting, and James says the outcome came from the Lord.
Jonah, a prophet (2 Kings 14:25), is a good name to know. But James doesn't mention him here. The man James names is Job, and he says, "You have heard of Job’s perseverance…"

That one sounds like it could fit after a man like Job, I'll give you that. But James doesn't say it here. Right after Job, he says, "The Lord is full of compassion and mercy." That's the line he lands on, and I'd hang my apron on it.

Boasting does come up elsewhere in James's letter (James 4:16), but not in this verse. Here he says, "Above all, my brothers, do not swear, not by heaven or earth or by any other oath." The word he uses is swear.

Helping those in need comes up elsewhere in James's letter (James 2:15–16), but it isn't his answer in this verse. He says, "Is anyone cheerful? He should sing praises." Singing praises is what the cheerful person is told to do.
Deacons are named in the New Testament (Philippians 1:1), but James doesn't mention them here. He says to call "…the elders of the church…" Those are the people the sick person calls.

Teachers are part of the church (Ephesians 4:11), but James doesn't name them here. He says the sick person should "…call the elders of the church to pray over him…" The elders are the ones he points to.
James does say it, so this one is true, friend. The elders are to "…pray over him and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord." The prayer and the oil are both right there in verse 14.

Humble sounds like it could belong at a sickbed, I'll give you that. But James says the prayer offered in faith "…will restore the one who is sick." Restore is the word he picks, and it's the one to bake with.
Forgiven. James says, "If he has sinned, he will be forgiven." It comes right after the Lord raises up the sick one. I like that the promise sits right next to the prayer.
A warning sounds like something a stern letter would say, I'll give you that. But James says, "If he has sinned, he will be forgiven." That's the promise he attaches, and it's a good one.

False is right. James says, "The prayer of a righteous man has great power to prevail." It isn't only prophets who pray with great power. He backs it up in the very next verse with Elijah, a prophet (1 Kings 18:36) whom he calls a man just like us (James 5:17).
The sun standing still was Joshua, Moses' assistant (Joshua 1:1), who spoke to the sun and moon in Joshua 10:12-13. That's a different man. James says Elijah prayed earnestly that it would not rain.
That's the sea Moses, Israel's leader, stretched his hand over in Exodus 14:21. But James is talking about Elijah, a prophet (1 Kings 18:36). He says Elijah prayed earnestly that it would not rain.
Weeks without rain would be dry, but James gives a much longer stretch. He says it did not rain on the land for three and a half years. That's years, friend.

Flowers would be a pretty ending, but James says something else. He says, "…the heavens gave rain, and the earth yielded its crops." Crops, the kind of thing a farmer waits for (James 5:7), is the word.

Trees would be a fine guess with all that rain coming down, but James doesn't name them. He says, "…the heavens gave rain, and the earth yielded its crops." Crops is what the earth gave, and that's the word I'm holding onto.

That's it. James says, "Whoever turns a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover over a multitude of sins." Bringing a wandering brother back matters a great deal to him. He puts real weight on it.

James doesn't talk about a title or a seat for the one who brings someone back. He says that person "…will save his soul from death…" What he names is a soul saved from death and a multitude of sins covered, not a position.
